a.answer: To achieve steady state concentration in short time
a.explanation: A loading dose rapidly attains the target steady-state plasma concentration without waiting ~4–5 half-lives. The other options are less precise: loading doses are most useful for drugs with LONG half-lives, and they reduce complications mainly by avoiding a prolonged subtherapeutic interval.

Clearance (Cl) is the parameter that quantifies the efficiency of irreversible drug removal from the body (volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time). Bioavailability, safety and volume of distribution describe other aspects of drug disposition.
In first-order kinetics, 50% of the drug is eliminated per half-life; after 4 half-lives ~93.75% has been eliminated, so ~93% is the best choice. (After 4 half-lives about 6.25% of the dose remains.)

Grapefruit juice irreversibly inhibits intestinal (and hepatic) CYP3A4, increasing the bioavailability/plasma levels of many drugs (e.g., statins, calcium-channel blockers). It is not an enzyme inducer and does not act on tubular secretion or reabsorption.

a.answer: Weak acids are absorbed efficiently across the cells of the stomach.
a.explanation: Weak acids are largely unionised in the acidic gastric milieu and therefore diffuse readily across gastric mucosal cells. Rectal drugs still partly bypass but do not 'completely' avoid first-pass effect, and most drugs are absorbed in the proximal small intestine; protein binding reduces, not enhances, absorption.

a.answer: An increase in the tissue concentrations of drug A
a.explanation: High-dose drug B displaces drug A from albumin-binding sites, raising the free (unbound) concentration of A; more free A distributes into tissues, increasing tissue concentrations and potentially toxicity. Bioavailability, half-life and Vd of A do not decrease as a result.

Of the options listed, cheese is the one associated with reduced metabolism of amine drugs — tyramine and related amines in aged cheese competitively inhibit monoamine oxidase. Cabbage, Brussels sprouts and charcoal-broiled food are classic ENZYME INDUCERS (CYP1A2) that increase drug metabolism.

Protein deficiency reduces the synthesis of drug-metabolising enzymes, so biotransformation (metabolism) proceeds at a lower rate, prolonging drug half-life. It does not shorten half-life or increase Vd.

Rapid acetylators generate larger amounts of the hepatotoxic metabolite (hydrazine) of isoniazid, predisposing them to drug-induced hepatitis. Slow acetylators are more prone to peripheral neuropathy.

cAMP mediates glycogen breakdown, smooth-muscle relaxation and lipolysis; in the heart, cAMP INCREASES heart rate (positive chronotropy) and contractility via PKA phosphorylation of calcium channels. A decreased heart rate is NOT a cAMP-mediated effect.

Corticosteroids act on intracellular (nuclear) receptors; the hormone–receptor complex dimerises and binds DNA response elements (glucocorticoid response elements) to regulate gene transcription. Acetylcholine, dopamine and diltiazem act via membrane receptors.

Receptors are regulatory proteins, and this class — including the four major receptor families (ligand-gated ion channels, G-protein-coupled, enzyme-linked and nuclear receptors) — is the best described and characterised class of drug targets. Enzymes, transport and structural proteins are distinct drug targets.

a.answer: A receptor for which no naturally occurring (endogenous) agent has been identified.
a.explanation: An 'orphan' receptor is one whose endogenous ligand has not yet been identified (e.g., many GPCRs awaiting deorphanisation). The other definitions describe receptors with unknown function or disease association, not 'orphan' status.

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic whose effect is physical (increases tubular fluid osmolarity) and is not mediated by a macromolecular receptor. Propranolol, prazosin and atenolol all act on adrenoceptors.

CYP3A4 metabolises the largest number of drugs (~50% of all marketed drugs) and is the site of many clinically dangerous drug interactions (e.g., macrolides/azoles inhibiting statin metabolism). CYP2C9, CYP2E1 and CYP1A2 have narrower substrate profiles.

a.answer: It generates the hepatotoxic metabolite N-acetyl benzoquinone imine from paracetamol
a.explanation: The hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) of paracetamol is generated mainly by CYP2E1 (with CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 contributing), NOT CYP2D6. CYP2D6 does demethylate codeine to morphine, hydroxylates metoprolol, and is inhibited by quinidine.

Microsomal enzyme induction increases the rate of drug metabolism, lowering plasma levels of the drug (and of co-administered drugs) and producing tolerance (metabolic/pharmacokinetic tolerance). Dependence and idiosyncrasy are not caused by enzyme induction.

Acetylation (e.g., of isoniazid, sulfonamides, hydralazine) occurs in the cytosol/mitochondria and is entirely non-microsomal. Glucuronide conjugation, oxidation and reduction are predominantly microsomal reactions.

a.answer: Extensively distributed to sites outside the vascular and interstitial spaces
a.explanation: A very large apparent volume of distribution (30 L/kg) indicates that the drug is extensively sequestered in tissues beyond plasma and interstitial fluid. Vd does not tell us about route of administration, mode of elimination, or ability to cross barriers.

a.answer: Area under the blood concentration-time curve (AUC)
a.explanation: AUC integrates the concentration of drug in blood over time and best reflects the total amount of drug reaching the systemic circulation (and, by extension, target tissues) after oral administration. Peak concentration and time-to-peak only capture single points.

When the enzyme (alcohol dehydrogenase) is saturated, elimination proceeds at a constant rate regardless of concentration — zero-order (saturation) kinetics. First-order elimination, clearance and redistribution describe different processes.

a.answer: To ensure that the drug concentration remains constant over time
a.explanation: Frequent dosing of a short half-life drug maintains plasma concentrations within the therapeutic window by replacing drug as it is eliminated, minimising peak-trough fluctuation. Steady state is achieved by any regular regimen after ~4–5 half-lives; frequency controls the fluctuation around it.

Steady-state concentration Css = (F × Dose) / (Cl × τ). If the oral dosing rate is constant but bioavailability (F) rises, Css increases proportionally. Half-life, elimination rate constant and clearance are not changed by the formulation.

Chronic administration induces the CYP enzyme that converts the pro-drug to its active form, so a given dose generates more active drug — the dose–response curve shifts left and potency increases. Efficacy (maximal effect) is unchanged.

Thiopentone is highly lipid-soluble: it rapidly enters the brain (onset of anaesthesia) and then redistributes into muscle and fat, terminating its effect — redistribution is a characteristic property of highly lipid-soluble drugs.

Cimetidine is a well-known INHIBITOR of microsomal enzymes (CYP450, especially CYP1A2 and CYP3A4), raising levels of co-administered drugs. Griseofulvin, rifampicin and phenobarbitone are enzyme inducers.

A Vd larger than total body water indicates extensive tissue sequestration/binding (the drug leaves plasma and concentrates in tissues), e.g., azithromycin, digoxin. Slow elimination, poor plasma solubility or high protein binding do not raise Vd above body water.

Penicillins are acidic drugs that bind extensively to serum albumin (about 60–90% bound) — the classic example of albumin binding. Lidocaine, propranolol and verapamil are basic drugs that bind mainly to α1-acid glycoprotein.

a.answer: It would be higher because of the first pass effect
a.explanation: Switching from IV to oral, the dose must be increased to compensate for hepatic first-pass extraction of the orally absorbed drug; only the fraction escaping first-pass metabolism reaches the systemic circulation.

The six manifestations (types) of Adverse Drug Reactions (ABCDEF classification):
• Type A – Augmented (dose-related): predictable, an exaggeration of the drug's pharmacological effect (e.g., hypoglycaemia with insulin, bleeding with warfarin).
• Type B – Bizarre (non-dose-related): unpredictable, allergic or idiosyncratic reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis to penicillin, aplastic anaemia with chloramphenicol).
• Type C – Chronic (dose-related and time-related): occur with long-term use (e.g., corticosteroid-induced osteoporosis, NSAID nephropathy).
• Type D – Delayed (time-related): appear after a delay, often long after exposure (e.g., carcinogenicity, teratogenicity — thalidomide).
• Type E – End of use (withdrawal): occur on stopping the drug (e.g., rebound hypertension after clonidine withdrawal, steroid withdrawal syndrome).
• Type F – Failure of therapy (treatment failure): the drug fails to produce the expected therapeutic effect (e.g., antimicrobial resistance, drug interactions reducing efficacy).

Overall bioavailability F = fraction absorbed × fraction escaping first-pass hepatic extraction.
Fraction absorbed = 70% = 0.70.
Hepatic extraction ratio (E) = 65% = 0.65, so fraction escaping the liver = 1 − E = 0.35.
F = 0.70 × 0.35 = 0.245 = 24.5%.
Answer: The overall bioavailability is 24.5%.

c.modelAnswer:
a) Branded vs Generic drug (8 marks):
• Branded (innovator) drug: marketed under a proprietary trade name by the company that developed it; usually more expensive; has patent protection during the exclusivity period.
• Generic drug: marketed under the international non-proprietary name (INN) or a non-proprietary brand; identical in active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route of administration and intended use; must be bioequivalent (same rate and extent of absorption) to the innovator product; usually cheaper because no development/marketing cost recovery.
• Both contain the same active pharmaceutical ingredient; the difference is in name, price and marketing, not in therapeutic effect if bioequivalent.
• Explain to the patient: 'The tablets contain the same medicine; the generic has a different name and costs less, but acts in the same way.'

b) Chemical name (2 marks):
The chemical name describes the drug's molecular structure according to chemical nomenclature rules (e.g., IUPAC name), e.g., N-acetyl-para-aminophenol for paracetamol. It is the scientific description of the molecule, too complex for everyday use.

c) Five ideal properties of drugs (5 marks) — any five:
1. Effectiveness — produces the desired therapeutic effect reliably.
2. Safety — no harmful or toxic effects at therapeutic doses (high therapeutic index).
3. Selectivity — acts only on the desired target/tissue with few off-target effects.
4. Reversibility — effects are reversible (antagonists/agonists can be counteracted).
5. Ease of administration — convenient route (oral preferred), acceptable to patients.
6. Freedom from drug interactions — does not interact adversely with other drugs/foods.
7. Low cost — affordable.
8. Chemical stability — stable in storage and in the body.
9. Simple generic name — easy to remember and prescribe.

Any three sources of drugs:
1. Plants (botanical): e.g., morphine and codeine (opium poppy), digoxin (Digitalis), quinine and artemisinin (antimalarials), atropine (belladonna), vincristine (periwinkle).
2. Animals: e.g., insulin (pancreas of ox/pig — historically), heparin (bovine lung/porcine intestine), thyroid extracts, conjugated estrogens (pregnant mare urine), enzymes such as pancreatin.
3. Microorganisms (fermentation): e.g., penicillin and cephalosporins (fungi), streptomycin, tetracyclines and macrolides (actinomycetes/bacteria).
4. Minerals: e.g., magnesium sulfate, iron salts, lithium carbonate, iodine, kaolin.
5. Synthetic (chemical synthesis): e.g., aspirin, paracetamol, sulfonamides, most modern drugs.
6. Recombinant DNA/biotechnology: e.g., human insulin, erythropoietin, growth hormone, monoclonal antibodies.

The four clinical phases of new drug development:
• Phase 1: First administration to humans — small number (20–100) of healthy volunteers (or sometimes patients). Purpose: safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion), maximum tolerated dose and dose-limiting toxicity.
• Phase 2: Therapeutic exploratory — 100–300 patients with the target disease. Purpose: preliminary evidence of efficacy, dose–response/optimal dose finding, short-term safety and common side effects.
• Phase 3: Therapeutic confirmatory — large trials (1,000–5,000+ patients), often randomised, controlled, multicentre, sometimes blinded, comparing the drug with placebo and/or standard treatment. Purpose: confirm efficacy, establish the benefit–risk (safety) profile and detect relatively common adverse reactions; data support registration/marketing authorisation.
• Phase 4: Post-marketing surveillance — after the drug is marketed, in the general population (thousands to millions). Purpose: detect rare, delayed or long-term adverse reactions, drug–drug interactions, special populations (pregnancy, children, elderly), new indications and pharmacovigilance reporting.
